History and Physical (H&P – Detailed)

Consult Summary:
27-year-old male stung on right arm by a bee/wasp a few minutes prior to call, reporting local rash and mild subjective breathing difficulty; no objective signs of anaphylaxis on video assessment. Managed as localized allergic reaction with safety-net advice and oral antihistamine recommendation.

History:
• Presenting complaint: Insect sting to right arm “a few minutes ago” with localized redness/blotchiness, puncture mark, soreness, and anxiety about possible allergic reaction.  
• Symptoms since sting:  
  – Subjective mild breathing difficulty and “weird” tongue sensation; denies severe dyspnea when questioned.  
  – Possible minimal right-sided lip swelling (not visible to clinician).  
• No chest pain, stridor, wheeze, generalized urticaria, dizziness, or syncope reported.  
• No prior history of anaphylaxis; never prescribed an epinephrine autoinjector.  
• Review of systems otherwise unremarkable.

Past Medical History:
• Eczema.  
• Occasional anxiety/panic episodes (never medicated).

Medications:
• None currently.  
Allergies:
• Penicillin (reaction details not documented).

Social History:
• Occupation: Computer scientist.  
• Lives alone; owns a cat.  
• Smoking, alcohol, recreational drug use: not discussed (missing).

Family History:
• No relevant familial illnesses or allergic reactions reported.

Physical Examination:
(Virtual assessment)  
• General: Alert, speaking full sentences, no respiratory distress.  
• Airway: Lips and oral cavity visually normal; no oropharyngeal swelling.  
• Respiratory: Breathing unlabored; no audible stridor or wheeze.  
• Skin: Right arm—small erythematous area with puncture mark; mild blotchy rash; no appreciable swelling.  
• Vitals: Not provided.

Investigations:
• None performed/available.

Assessment & Plan:
Issue 1 – Localized allergic reaction to insect sting  
  • Plan:  
    – Begin oral antihistamine: Chlorphenamine 4 mg tab (OTC) up to six times daily or once-daily non-sedating antihistamine (dose/route/frequency not documented).  
    – Monitor sting site; seek care if erythema spreads, becomes hot, or suggests infection (possible need for antibiotics).  
    – Provide patient education link on anaphylaxis signs/symptoms.  
    – Advise immediate ED attendance or emergency services if any red-flag features develop (lip/tongue swelling, breathing difficulty, stridor, widespread rash, dizziness).  
    – No routine allergy testing at this time; reconsider if recurrent reactions occur.

Issue 2 – Anxiety surrounding possible allergic reaction  
  • Plan:  
    – Reassurance regarding current benign clinical picture.  
    – Encourage low threshold to re-consult if anxious or symptoms change.

General Plan items:  
• No other issues raised.  
• Follow-up: Patient to self-monitor; contact service or present to ED as per safety-net advice.

Quality checks:
• Missing expected elements: vital signs, full medication list, smoking/alcohol history.  
• No internal conflicts noted.  
• Transcript quality: Clear; minor filler words, no inaudible sections affecting clinical content.
